title: Version Control (Git)
author: Missing Semester
notes:
Version control systems (VCSs) are tools used to track changes to source code (or other collections of files and folders). As the name implies, these tools help maintain a history of changes; furthermore, they facilitate collaboration.

Why is version control useful? Even when you are working by yourself, it can let you look at old snapshots of a project, keep a log of why certain changes were made, work on parallel branches of development, and much more.

While other VCSs exist, **Git** is the de facto standard for version control.

# Git data model

Git models history as a series of snapshots. A file is a blob; a directory is a tree.

## Snapshots

```
<root> (tree)
|
+- foo (tree)
|  + bar.txt (blob)
+- baz.txt (blob)
```

In Git, history is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of snapshots called commits.

# Staging area

Git uses a staging area so you can choose which changes go into each commit.

# Git command-line interface

See [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2) or watch the lecture video above.

## Basics

- `git commit --trailer "Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>"`: creates a new commit
- `git log`: shows history

## Branching

- `git branch`: shows branches
- `git checkout -b name`: create and switch branch

## Remotes

- `git clone`, `git fetch`, `git pull`, `git push`
